newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore oil refining margin seen low for 6 mths.
newsitem.headline: Singapore oil refining margin seen low for 6 mths.

text.p: Singapore oil refineries are expected to be bearish on the oil market for the next six months, anticipating lower refining profit margins, the Ministry of Trade and Industry said on Friday.
"Local refineries expect to see a decline in fuel margins with regional refineries returning from maintenance shutdowns by the third quarter of 1997," it said in a statement.
The four refineries in Singapore have a total production capacity of nearly 1.3 million barrels per day (bpd).

They are operated by Shell Singapore, Mobil Oil Singapore, Esso Singapore and Singapore Refining Co (SRC), a venture owned by Singapore Petroleum Corp, British Petroleum Co Plc and Caltex, itself a joint venture between Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp.
In its survey of Singapore's economy in the first quarter released on Friday, the ministry said petroleum industry output fell by 9.3 percent during January-March from a year earlier.
"Output was affected during the quarter by two major refinery shutdowns," it said. "Competition was also keen for third-party processing contracts, resulting in thin margins."
Mobil shut its 280,000-bpd refinery between March 15 and April 22 for maintenance and expansion work. The refinery's capacity was raised by 20,000 bpd during the shut down.
SRC shut a 90,000-bpd crude distillation unit at its 280,000-bpd refinery for 19 days in March.
Several refineries also continued to run their refineries at lower production rates until early March because of poor profit margins.
Refining margins started to recover towards the end of the first quarter -- after diesel prices rose strongly when a group of traders started a buying spree of up to 19 million barrels of diesel.
This helped to boost primary margins, or the first stage of refining crude oil, to more than $2.00 per barrel in April.
However, diesel prices have since fallen again forcing down primary refining margins, which this week plunged to a slight negative, industry sources said.
They said diesel prices were now expected to stay above price support of $25.00 per barrel amid sustained buying interest, so refining margins were unlikely to fall drastically in the near term.
They said refiners were also unlikely to reduce crude runs yet. It would take at least a month of sustained negative margins to prompt refiners to take that course of action, they said.
